facts.statement: The genus Gemuendina was named by Traquair in 1903.
The species Gemuendina stuertzi is the type species of the genus.
Broilina heroldi, described by Stensiö in 1971, is a synonym of Gemuendina.
Gemuendina stuertzi was a placoderm found in the seas of Early Devonian Germany.
facts.quote: Gemuendina stuertzi (named for Gemünden from where it was discovered) is a placoderm of the order Rhenanida, of the seas of Early Devonian Germany.

facts.statement: Gemuendina had a body shape resembling a scaly ray with an upturned head.
facts.quote: In life, Gemuendina resembled a scaly ray with an upturned head, or a large-finned stargazer.

facts.statement: Gemuendina had its eyes and nostrils positioned on top of its head facing upward.
facts.quote: Unlike rays, however, both Gemuendina`s eyes and nostrils were placed atop the head, facing upward.

facts.statement: Gemuendina is considered an example of convergent evolution due to its superficial similarity to rays.
facts.quote: G. stuertzi is often invoked as an example of convergent evolution- with its flat body and huge, wing-like pectoral fins it has a strong, albeit superficial similarity to rays.

facts.statement: Gemuendina's upturned mouth allowed it to suction prey swimming overhead, unlike modern rays.
facts.quote: Furthermore, G. stuertzis upturned mouth would have enabled it to suction prey that swam overhead, rather than swallow sediment or suction prey out of the substrate like modern rays.

facts.statement: The fragile armor of Gemuendina means few intact examples have survived in the fossil record.
facts.quote: Because their armor was so fragile, few intact examples of rhenanids have survived in the fossil record.

facts.statement: Intact, nearly pristine specimens of Gemuendina were preserved in the anoxic Hunsruck lagerstätte.
facts.quote: Because several regions of the Hunsruck lagerstätte were anoxic, thus free of scavenging organisms, intact, nearly pristine (albeit flattened) specimens of G. stuertzi have been found as a result.

facts.statement: Gemuendina lacked tooth plates and instead used star-shaped tubercle scales to seize and swallow prey.
facts.quote: Also unlike other placoderms, it did not have the characteristic tooth plates of placoderms. Instead, it had star-shaped tubercle scales that allowed it to seize, then swallow fish and other animals that swam too close with its mouth.

facts.statement: Specimens of Gemuendina stuertzi ranged from 30 to 100 centimeters in length.
facts.quote: Specimens of G. stuertzi ranged in size from 30 to 100 centimeters in length.

facts.statement: Erik Stensiö described a one-meter long specimen as the species Broilina heroldi in 1971.
facts.quote: In 1971, Erik Stensiö described a metre long specimen as a new species, "Broilina heroldi," which was later synonymized with Gemuendina.

facts.statement: The parent group of Gemuendina is Asterosteidae.
Gemuendina belongs to the family Asterosteidae.
Gemuendina is classified in the class Placodermi.
Gemuendina lived during the Emsian stage, from 410.62 to 399.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Emsian to Emsian (410.62 to 399.5 million years ago)

rejected.statement: Gemuendina had armor composed of a mosaic of unfused bony plates and scales, unlike other placoderm orders.
rejected.quote: Unlike most other placoderm orders, such as the antiarchs or arthrodires, Gemuendina and its four other known relatives (or seven, if the three species of the ichthyolith genus Ohioaspis are confirmed to be rhenanids) had armor made up of a mosaic of unfused bony plates and scales.
